title: The Romaniotes
hookLine: Greek-speaking Jews of Greece, with their own prayers since ancient times

cards: In the town of Ioannina, in the mountains of northwestern Greece, a lake sits below an old stone fortress. Inside the walls, down a quiet lane, is a whitewashed synagogue. Most of the year its doors are closed.
Then, in summer, families arrive from Athens, from Israel, from New York, and the old benches fill again. Some of the prayers sung there come from a tradition that is neither Sephardic nor Ashkenazi.

teach.b: The Romaniotes are the Jews of the Greek-speaking world, who lived there long before Jews arrived from Spain. The Tanakh already knows Greece.
In the list of nations in Genesis, among the sons of Japheth, is Javan, the Hebrew name for Greece. Romaniote Jews spoke Greek.
Some wrote Greek in Hebrew letters, and they had their own prayer book, their own liturgical poems and their own customs.
When Jews expelled from Spain arrived in Greek lands, they brought Ladino and Sephardic customs, and in many cities the older Romaniote ways were absorbed into the new.
Ioannina was different. There the Romaniote rite held on, and the synagogue inside the fortress kept its old prayers and melodies. The Holocaust reached Ioannina too.
Its Jews were rounded up and deported, and few came back. After the war, the community that remained was tiny. But the descendants did not forget.
In New York, Romaniote families from Ioannina built their own synagogue, Kehila Kedosha Janina, on the Lower East Side, and it still holds services.
In Ioannina, the old synagogue opens for prayer and remembrance, and families return to stand in it.
The Romaniotes are a reminder that the map of Jewish life has more than two colors.

how: Romaniote families gather at the synagogue in Ioannina for summer services and remembrance, and Kehila Kedosha Janina in New York holds services and keeps a small museum of Romaniote life.

games.q: you are a Romaniote Jew in Ioannina. Jews from Spain arrive with new customs. what does your town do?
games.why: in many cities the older ways were absorbed, but Ioannina held on to its Romaniote prayers and melodies.

practice: Picture the fortress above the lake and the whitewashed synagogue, closed most of the year, then the summer day its doors open.
Hold in mind those who did not come back after the war, and those who keep returning; if you pray, remember them both in your own words.
